subject: Will IT managers accept the new shiny server?

messages.author: 18dfb1393eda7b0e
messages.subject: Will IT managers accept the new shiny server?
parts:
I'm very impressed with shiny. This post voices my concerns about picking shiny as a base technology for a project. As with everything, there are trade offs and I see may benefits of using shiny. One "con" is an apparent lack of some widgets we might need, but I'm not worried about that because I believe the issue will be addressed by the community as time goes on. Maybe I'll even be able to contribute!

What I'm worried about is building the application and then hitting a wall of resistance when I try to deploy the application in a real-world situation. By real-world, I mean on a publicly facing agency-owned web server. I'm concerned that network managers will not agree to install the shiny server and/or not allow access to port 3838 through the routers. Apache is both open source and a known player. I think that an application frame work that uses Apache plus php or similar technologies would be an easy sell, 

The shiny server free edition is open source and would likely meet my fundamental needs in many respects. In my case, the ui.R and server.R code would be public domain along with most of the data and there will not be a large user base. 

However, this server (and even the pro edition) is not well understood. I can hear the IT guys say: "shiny-what? and no we will not open port 3838 of incoming connections" ... followed by anther comment asking for the budget number for the $10,000 licence for the pro version and then being passed off once again to the "Department of No" (every organization has at least one of these departments, but we seem to have 10 of them). 

It is more likely that I'd be able to run FastRWeb, at least I would very much like to hear comments from this forum on that alternative with respect to dealing with IT.

What I'm asking here is this: are my concerns shared by others and how have others addressed them? Are there some technical solutions that can be used to address the issues? 

I'm really hoping that my concerns can be set aside as the benefits to shiny seem huge to me. I applaud the group that developed it!

Thanks in advance!

Cheers, Nick Crookston

messages.author: 9711d30301c32133
messages.subject: Re: Will IT managers accept the new shiny server?
parts:
Hi Nick,

Thanks for starting this discussion; I'm interested to see how others in the community feel about these concerns. I'll throw out my 2 cents.

First, the port 3838 issue is merely one of configuration. Shiny Server Open Source is easily capable of running on whatever port(s) your organization feel is appropriate (including 80). (http://rstudio.github.io/shiny-server/os/latest/#default-configuration)

While we happen not to use Apache or PHP, we are based on similar open source and battle-tested frameworks. Our hope with the advent of our installers is that we could take a lot of the uncertainty out of the process of setting up Shiny Server. Just a couple of commands will get you a fully configured Shiny Server instance (though you certainly have the power to change directories, ports, and a myriad of other options as you see fit).

I completely understand that many organizations are wary of new technologies (I've been there!). Our goal with Shiny Server Pro is to alleviate some of those concerns and make R feel a bit more accessible -- precisely for audiences like IT managers. Check out the screenshots (by clicking on the small cameras in the comparison table) on the Shiny Server page. The idea is to present IT groups who may have never heard of R -- let alone Shiny Server -- with a familiar dashboard that they can understand. This way, without ever having to touch R, an administrator can get in and inspect/manage/kill the various applications and processes running on the server.

If you're in a spot to setup and administer the server yourself and you're not in need of any of the Enterprise features offered in Pro, I'd say put the Open Source edition on port 80 and, as far as your IT group is concerned, you're just running another web application. If you're looking for your IT group to be comfortable administrating the server or if you're in need of the expanded features in Pro, then you can go that route. We've had multiple sales calls with IT groups who were initially hesitant about "this new R thing" and walked away feeling comfortable with the product. We'd be happy to have someone run through the product with your IT team, if you'd like. Just reach out at sa...@rstudio.com

Best,
Jeff
